title: Character Portraits Second Pass
author: Dead_Fox_7
selftext: Was happy with a post I made last week showing seasons of a game concept but had several callouts about the character portraits so I decided to give them a second pass. Happy with the results so far. These were mainly created in Seedream 5 with some post Photoshop love.

comments.author: mccoypauley
comments.body:
Why not try to choose a style that deviates strongly from the median AI generators produce?

For example, I use local SDXL and select a combination of artist tokens to approximate a new style, that way it doesn't default to the standard that's depicted in your before and after. It's not hard to set up a local model and experiment.

replies.author: CrusherEAGLE
replies.body: Would you mind elaborating a bit, please?

replies.author: mccoypauley
replies.body:
Sure—so you can install ComfyUI on your local machine and download open source image models. There are lots out there, and they all run on decent cards, though a 3090 at least is good.

Many modern models: Qwen, Chroma, Flux, etc are out there and they can generate art that’s just as good as stuff you can make with ChatGPT or Midjourney, etc. The modern models have good prompt comprehension and adherence in plain language. They are not as good at doing plain language editing like Chat/Gemini, but with enough tooling in ComfyUI you can approximate most of what you can do with the hosted frontier models.

However! The modern models all don’t understand artist tokens anymore. Not at the level of fidelity that older models from 2022-2023 did. SDXL was the last one that could do this properly. You can get genuinely unique looking art by combining a bunch of artist tokens and teasing out a replicable style this way, and I use this method to brand projects uniquely. The result is that you can’t tell that it’s AI generated because it lacks the hallmarks of “median” output that modern models tend to generate. That is: modern models out-the-box produce pretty people, super coherent, glossy CGI or Ghibli-esque/comic superhero style art by default. It’s a consequence of averaged output. It’s even worse with ChatGPT and Gemini, less so with Midjourney because there’s a lot of options to get wilder stuff in their platform.

Now, you *can* get the modern models to be faithful to artist tokens, but it involves training them on the artist in question’s work, to produce LoRAs that add knowledge of the artist to the model you’re using. The problem is that it’s insanely inefficient, since old models like SDXL already understood “Edward Gorey” and what his style is implicitly. You can prompt artist tokens in modern models, but their styles are these weak approximations.

So today, modern models are less smart about artist styles because of a combination of abandoning the diffusion architecture and their creators wanting to protect IP/avoid legal dispute.

What I tend to do is stage composition in newer models and then bring that into SDXL, but even three years later, the new models haven’t been beat by the creativity/variability of old ones. And hosted ones like Chat and Gemini are absolute trash by comparison. MJ is good but its prompt comprehension sucks.

replies.author: DrEndGame
replies.body:
Would you have examples of your output? 

And what you tend to do is to use a new model then have SDXL translate that into an artist token? Or something else? Apologies confused on how you have the modern models with SDXL interact.

replies.author: mccoypauley
replies.body:
Sure thing, I am out of state right now but when I get home on Sunday I can share some comparisons as an example.

The pipeline from modern to SDXL is tough because the more fully realized an image is coming from a modern model, the less influence SDXL can have over it. There are three approaches:

\- simple image to image, but this is the least effective because then modern image-as-input is fully realized

\- controlnets. That is, use a modern image as a source and then reconstruct it with controlnets in SDXL (meaning it converts the image into outlines as a sort of paint by numbers). Better, but not as good as just generating it in SDXL to begin with

\- generate a low fidelity outline in a modern model to take advantage of its prompt adherence, then feed that to a ComfyUI pipeline that ultimately renders it in SDXL

These days I tend to do the work in SDXL and use frontier models to make corrections.

replies.author: mccoypauley
replies.body: ComfyUI is free and so are all the local models you can download. You just need a decent video card (3090 or higher, though you can technically run it on crappier cards.)
